caseNotes: You have not ordered anything this month.
lessons: Connect a common scam outcome to the security principle it violates.
Recognize the common signs of a fake delivery text: unexpected, urgent, a small fee and an odd link.
Name phishing and spot a lookalike domain.
Treat an OTP like a key: never share it, and verify callers through a channel you choose.
Recognize that a request to disable security tools is a red flag.
Recognize that harmless-looking posts can collect personal data.

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 3: Fundamentals of Information Security (CIA Triad)
questions.explanation: Confidentiality means only authorized people can see information. The scammer was never authorized, so confidentiality is broken. Integrity would be broken if the scammer changed her data, and availability if she were locked out. Being tricked into giving the password away does not make the access authorized.
questions.feedback: Correct. A stolen password breaks confidentiality: someone who shouldn't see your data now can.
questions.learningObjective: Connect a common scam outcome to the security principle it violates.
choices: Availability
Integrity
Confidentiality
None, because she typed it in herself
questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.body: Ana typed her student login into a fake "school portal" page. The scammer can now read her grades, messages and personal details. Which part of the CIA Triad was broken?
questions.hint: Think about what happened to Ana's information: was it changed, locked away, or seen by someone who shouldn't see it?

inspectables.label: The page
inspectables.finding: It only looks like the school portal. Whatever Ana typed went straight to the scammer.

inspectables.match: read her grades, messages and personal details
inspectables.label: What the scammer can do
inspectables.finding: The scammer can now look at Ana's private information. Was anything changed or locked - or only seen?

evidence.title: Fake login page
evidence.whyItMatters: Fake pages copy real ones to collect what you type.

evidence.title: Private details exposed
evidence.whyItMatters: Someone who isn't allowed can now read Ana's information.

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 16: Information Security Best Practices (user awareness)
questions.explanation: You are not expecting a package. It comes from a regular mobile number, sets a 12-hour deadline, and links to a domain that isn't the courier's. The small fee is bait: the real goal is your card or e-wallet details. Couriers don't collect fees through random text links.
questions.feedback: Scam. No order, a small 'fee' and a 12-hour deadline. They want your payment details, not ₱29.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize the common signs of a fake delivery text: unexpected, urgent, a small fee and an odd link.
questions.body: SwiftParcel: Your package is ON HOLD due to an incomplete address. Pay the ₱29 redelivery fee within 12 hours or it will be returned:
questions.scenarioContext: You have not ordered anything this month.
questions.hint: Compare the text with your case notes: were you expecting a package? Then check who sent it and where the link goes.

inspectables.label: Sender
inspectables.finding: An ordinary mobile number, not a named courier. Real delivery companies text from their own name or a short code.

inspectables.label: The claim
inspectables.finding: Your case notes say you haven't ordered anything this month - so which package?

inspectables.label: The request
inspectables.finding: A small fee is bait: the real goal is your card or e-wallet details.

inspectables.label: Deadline
inspectables.finding: A short deadline pushes you to act before you think.

inspectables.label: Link
inspectables.finding: swiftparcel-redeliver.example is not an official courier site, and it starts with http (not secure).

evidence.title: Ordinary mobile number
evidence.whyItMatters: Couriers don't text from random mobile numbers.

evidence.title: No order to deliver
evidence.whyItMatters: You haven't ordered anything, so there is no real package.

evidence.title: Asks for a payment
evidence.whyItMatters: Small fees are used to steal card and e-wallet details.

evidence.title: Pressure to act fast
evidence.whyItMatters: Scams rush you so you don't stop to check.

evidence.title: Unofficial, insecure link
evidence.whyItMatters: The link isn't the courier's site and isn't secure.

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Introduction to Computer Security: "types of security threats… in both personal and organizational contexts"
questions.explanation: It pretends to be a trusted sender, creates fear with "deleted in 24 hours", and asks you to sign in through a link. That combination is phishing. The domain is a lookalike: uphs1 with the number 1 in place of the letter l. Real storage warnings don't need you to "verify" your password through an email link.
questions.feedback: Phishing. Look closely: uphs1, not uphsl. A fake sender plus a fake deadline plus 'sign in here' means phishing.
questions.learningObjective: Name phishing and spot a lookalike domain.
choices: Phishing
Ransomware
Denial-of-service attack
A normal storage warning
questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.body: Email from: Campus IT Helpdesk <helpdesk@uphs1-binan.example> Subject: Mailbox 98% full: verify now "Your school mailbox will be DELETED in 24 hours. Click below and sign in to verify your account." What kind of threat is this?
questions.hint: Check the sender's address letter by letter, then ask yourself what the email wants you to do.

inspectables.label: Sender address
inspectables.finding: Look closely: uphs1 uses the number 1 instead of the letter l. It's a lookalike of the school's real domain.

inspectables.label: Subject
inspectables.finding: Full mailboxes really happen. On its own this isn't a warning sign - look at what the email asks you to do.

inspectables.label: Threat
inspectables.finding: A scary deadline pushes you to act fast without checking.

inspectables.match: sign in to verify your account
inspectables.label: What it asks
inspectables.finding: It wants your password through a link. Real IT staff never ask you to 'verify' your password by email.

evidence.title: Lookalike sender domain
evidence.whyItMatters: uphs1 is not uphsl - a fake address made to look real.

evidence.title: Scary deadline
evidence.whyItMatters: Threats and short deadlines are pressure tactics.

evidence.title: Asks you to sign in through a link
evidence.whyItMatters: That's how fake pages collect passwords.

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Authentication and Access Control
questions.explanation: A one-time code (OTP) proves that you are approving something. Whoever has it can approve a login or payment as you, so the caller is probably the one making the transaction. A real bank never asks you to read an OTP aloud. Calling back on a number you already trust is the safe way to check.
questions.feedback: Hang up. No real bank asks for your OTP. Call back using the number on your card.
questions.learningObjective: Treat an OTP like a key: never share it, and verify callers through a channel you choose.
choices: Read the code quickly to stop the fraud
Give only the first three digits
Ask them to email you instead
Hang up and call the number on the back of your card or in the official app
questions.subject: What Should You Do?
questions.body: A caller says: "This is ExampleBank's fraud department. Someone is using your card right now. We just sent you a 6-digit code. Read it to me so we can block the transaction."
questions.hint: Who should ever see your one-time code? And how could you check that the caller is really your bank?

inspectables.label: Who they say they are
inspectables.finding: Anyone can claim to be your bank on the phone. You didn't call them - they called you.

inspectables.label: Pressure
inspectables.finding: Creating panic stops you from thinking clearly.

inspectables.label: The request
inspectables.finding: That code is your one-time password (OTP). Whoever has it can approve logins and payments as you.

evidence.title: Unverified caller
evidence.whyItMatters: A caller's name or claim proves nothing.

evidence.title: Panic and urgency
evidence.whyItMatters: Urgency is used to stop you from checking.

evidence.title: Asks for your OTP
evidence.whyItMatters: No real bank ever asks you to read out a one-time code.

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Malware and Threats: "preventing, detecting, and removing malware, including… anti-malware tools"
questions.explanation: Asking you to turn off your antivirus is a major warning sign: the file is built to get past it. Fake "generators" are a common way to spread trojans and information stealers, which take saved passwords and logged-in sessions. Scanning afterwards is too late, and sending it to a friend puts them at risk.
questions.feedback: Don't run it. Anyone who asks you to switch off your antivirus is trying to get past it.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize that a request to disable security tools is a red flag.
choices: Turn off the antivirus just for a minute and run it
Run it, then scan your PC afterwards
Don't download it, and block or report the sender
Send it to a friend to test first
questions.subject: Scenario-Based
questions.body: A stranger in a gaming chat sends you FreeSkins_Generator.exe and says: "Turn off your antivirus first. It gives a false alarm on this tool."
questions.hint: Why would a safe program need your antivirus switched off?

inspectables.match: A stranger in a gaming chat
inspectables.label: Sender
inspectables.finding: You don't know this person, and the offer came out of nowhere.

inspectables.label: The file
inspectables.finding: .exe files are programs that run on your computer. Free 'generators' are a common way to spread malware.

inspectables.label: The request
inspectables.finding: A real tool never needs your protection switched off. Malware does.

evidence.title: Unknown sender
evidence.whyItMatters: Files from strangers can't be trusted.

evidence.title: A program file
evidence.whyItMatters: Running an .exe gives it control of your computer.

evidence.title: Asks you to disable antivirus
evidence.whyItMatters: That request exists to get malware past your protection.

questions.curriculumRef: Social and Professional Issues (BIT2105) — Weeks 10–11: Ethics for IT Users ("responsible use of… social media")
questions.explanation: Pet names, childhood streets and birth months are common answers to account security questions. Posting them publicly gives scammers what they need to reset your passwords or make an impersonation more convincing. The "game" is how they collect the answers.
questions.feedback: Data harvesting. Those are classic security-question answers. Don't post them.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize that harmless-looking posts can collect personal data.
questions.subject: FIND YOUR STAR NAME
questions.body: Comment your first pet's name + the street you grew up on + your birth month!
questions.scenarioContext: Is this harmless fun or a scam? LEGITIMATE = harmless fun, SCAM = data harvesting.
questions.hint: Look at the three things the post asks for. Where else are those exact answers used?

inspectables.label: Who posted it
inspectables.finding: A viral post from someone you don't know. It's made to be shared widely.

inspectables.label: Where you answer
inspectables.finding: Comments are public. Anyone - including scammers - can read them.

inspectables.label: It asks for
inspectables.finding: A very common answer to account security questions.

inspectables.label: It asks for
inspectables.finding: Another classic security-question answer.

inspectables.label: It asks for
inspectables.finding: Part of your birthday, which is often used to confirm who you are.

evidence.title: Public answers
evidence.whyItMatters: Anything posted in comments is visible to everyone.

evidence.title: Security-question answers
evidence.whyItMatters: These answers are used to reset passwords.

evidence.title: Personal details
evidence.whyItMatters: Birthdays help scammers pretend to be you.

rooms.briefing:
You just joined the Cybercrime Investigation Unit. Scammers send fake texts, emails and posts to steal money, passwords and personal details, and your job is to catch them.

This first room is your training case. A guide will show you how to investigate, use hints and answer. Six questions are waiting, and they arrive in a different order every time you play.
objectives: Follow the guide on your first question.
Answer all six questions in this room.
Score {unlock} or more to unlock the next room.

caseNotes: While browsing, a full-screen red page appeared and started beeping.
One minute before this email arrived, you clicked "Forgot password" on NovaCloud yourself. Trusted domain (case files): novacloud.example
lessons: Check whether a request for personal data is proportional and explained before handing it over.
Value accounts by what else they unlock.
Know where real security alerts and updates come from.
Preserve and document evidence before doing anything else.
Avoid "everything is a scam" thinking: confirm real messages with evidence.
Find the real domain in a URL by reading right to left.

questions.curriculumRef: Social and Professional Issues (BIT2105) — Week 15: Data Privacy Act (RA 10173)
questions.explanation: The Data Privacy Act's principles include transparency (tell people why data is collected), legitimate purpose and proportionality (collect only what is needed). A raffle needs a way to contact you, not your ID and birthdate, and an ID photo plus a birthdate can be used for identity theft. With no notice, you can't know what happens to your data.
questions.feedback: An ID photo for a raffle? Too much. Ask why they need it and look for a privacy notice.
questions.learningObjective: Check whether a request for personal data is proportional and explained before handing it over.
choices: They ask for a photo of your ID and your birthdate just to join, and there is no privacy notice explaining why
The raffle is free to join
The staff wear company shirts
The draw is next week
questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.body: A raffle booth at the mall asks you to fill in a form to join. Which of these is the biggest privacy warning sign?

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 9: Information Assets and Asset Management ("evaluate their value and protection requirements")
questions.explanation: Most services send password resets to your email. Whoever controls that inbox can reset the passwords of your other accounts, including social media, e-wallets and school accounts. That makes it your most valuable information asset, so it needs a unique password and MFA first.
questions.feedback: Your email is the master key. Every 'Forgot password' link goes there.
questions.learningObjective: Value accounts by what else they unlock.
choices: Your online game account
Your main email account, which receives password-reset links
Your music streaming account
An old forum account you no longer use
questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.body: Which of your accounts deserves the strongest protection, because a scammer who controls it can take over many of your other accounts?

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Operating System Security ("patch management, and security configuration")
questions.explanation: This is a tech-support scam. Real security warnings and updates come from your operating system's own settings and security app, not from a web page with a phone number. The "support" agent will ask for remote access or payment. Close the tab. If it won't close, end the browser with Task Manager.
questions.feedback: Scam. Real alerts come from your system settings, never from a web page asking you to call.
questions.learningObjective: Know where real security alerts and updates come from.
questions.subject: SYSTEM SECURITY ALERT
questions.body: Your computer is INFECTED and LOCKED. Call Certified Support at 1-800-555-0199 now. DO NOT restart your computer.
questions.scenarioContext: While browsing, a full-screen red page appeared and started beeping.

questions.curriculumRef: Cyber Forensics (BIT2226) — Digital Evidence and Evidence Collection ("collection, preservation, and documentation")
questions.explanation: Evidence is what lets the platform, your e-wallet and the police act. Reference numbers and the seller's account details can help trace the money. Deleting the chat destroys proof. Public threats can backfire on you legally. "Pay more to get a refund" is a second scam.
questions.feedback: Save the evidence first: chat, profile and reference number. Then report it.
questions.learningObjective: Preserve and document evidence before doing anything else.
choices: Delete the chat so you can move on
Post the seller's photo and threaten them publicly
Send another payment because they say it "unlocks" your refund
Save screenshots of the chat, the seller's profile link and the payment receipt with its reference number, then report to PayLite and the authorities
questions.subject: What Should You Do?
questions.body: You paid ₱1,500 to an online seller through PayLite. The seller then blocked you and never shipped. What should you do first?

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Weeks 7–8: Principles of Information Assurance (authentication)
questions.explanation: You started this action yourself a minute ago. The sender and link domain match the trusted domain exactly. The email doesn't ask for your password or any personal details, and it tells you it's safe to ignore if you didn't ask for it. A reset email that proves you own the inbox is how authentication is supposed to work.
questions.feedback: Legitimate. You asked for it, the domain matches, and it doesn't ask for your password.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid "everything is a scam" thinking: confirm real messages with evidence.
questions.subject: Password reset request
questions.body: We received a request to reset your password. This link expires in 15 minutes. If you didn't request this, you can ignore this email.
questions.scenarioContext: One minute before this email arrived, you clicked "Forgot password" on NovaCloud yourself. Trusted domain (case files): novacloud.example

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Web and Application Security
questions.explanation: A domain is read from the right, ending just before the first single "/". Here that is account-verify.example, and everything to its left is a subdomain the attacker chose. This is not typosquatting, because nothing is misspelled. HTTPS only encrypts the connection (see M03).
questions.feedback: Read the domain right to left: account-verify.example. The bank's name is just a decoy subdomain.
questions.learningObjective: Find the real domain in a URL by reading right to left.
choices: It's ExampleBank's site because "examplebank" appears first
It's safe because it uses HTTPS
It's a subdomain trick: the real domain is account-verify.example
It's a misspelled (typosquatted) bank domain
questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.body: A message links to: https://examplebank.example.account-verify.example/login. Which is true?

rooms.intro: The traps are getting more convincing.
lessons: Correct the common belief that a padlock means a site is safe.
Recognize impersonation that relies on emotion and urgency, and verify through a known channel.
Report honestly and quickly after a security mistake.
Pick the control that matches the threat.
Spot fake hotspots and understand the limits of VPNs.
Learn that what a phone displays is not proof of who sent a message.

questions.curriculumRef: Advanced Cybersecurity Strategies (BIT4233). Supporting: Computer Security (BIT1225), Cryptography — Modern Cryptography ("secure data in transit and at rest")
questions.explanation: HTTPS (TLS) protects data in transit so others on the network can't read or change it. Certificates are easy for anyone to get for their own domain, so scam sites often have padlocks too. The padlock tells you the connection is private, not who you're talking to. You still have to check the domain.
questions.feedback: The padlock means encrypted, not trustworthy. Fake sites have padlocks too. Check the domain.
questions.learningObjective: Correct the common belief that a padlock means a site is safe.
choices: The site is owned by the real company
Data between you and this site is encrypted, but the site itself could still be fake
The site has been checked by the government
The site cannot contain malware
questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.body: A login page shows a padlock and starts with https://. What does the padlock actually prove?

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Weeks 10–11: Cybersecurity Threats and Attack Landscape
questions.explanation: The sender claims to be family on a "new number", invents an emergency, asks for money, and blocks you from checking ("don't call yet"). That is social engineering: it exploits trust and urgency rather than technology. To check, call Migs's old number or ask something only the real Migs would know.
questions.feedback: Impersonation. New number + emergency + 'don't call' means: call the old number first.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize impersonation that relies on emotion and urgency, and verify through a known channel.
choices: Impersonation ("new number" family emergency) social engineering
Malware infection
A data breach
A promotional spam message
questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.body: SMS from an unknown number: "Ma, si Migs 'to. Nasira phone ko, bagong number ko 'to. Pa-send naman ₱3,000 sa PayLite 0917 555 0188, emergency lang. Wag ka muna tumawag, wala pa akong load." What attack is this?

questions.curriculumRef: Social and Professional Issues (BIT2105). Supporting: IAS Week 16 (incident reporting procedures) — Weeks 13–14: Security Incidents ("recommend appropriate preventive and corrective measures")
questions.explanation: Fast reporting limits the damage: IT can lock sessions, block the site and warn others. Changing the password quickly makes the stolen one useless. Hiding the mistake is unprofessional and gives the attacker time. Forwarding spreads the dangerous link. Deleting it removes evidence IT needs.
questions.feedback: Report it. Mistakes happen, and hiding them is what makes them serious.
questions.learningObjective: Report honestly and quickly after a security mistake.
choices: Say nothing, since nothing bad has happened yet
Forward the email to coworkers to ask if they got it too
Delete the email so no one finds out
Change the password through the official site right away, report to IT with the email, and watch for login or MFA prompts you didn't start
questions.subject: What Should You Do?
questions.body: During your OJT, you typed your work password into a page you opened from an email. A minute later, you notice the address was wrong.

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 15: Security Controls and Protection Mechanisms ("administrative, technical, and physical controls")
questions.explanation: MFA is a technical control: the attacker needs a second factor (an app prompt, code or security key) as well as the password. The other choices don't affect a remote login. MFA is not perfect: only approve prompts that you started yourself.
questions.feedback: MFA. A stolen password alone isn't enough, if you never approve a prompt you didn't start.
questions.learningObjective: Pick the control that matches the threat.
choices: A stronger Wi-Fi password at home
A privacy screen protector
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) on the account
Clearing the browser history
questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.body: A classmate's school account password was stolen through phishing. Which control is most likely to stop the attacker from logging in?

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Network Security ("firewalls, intrusion detection/prevention systems (IDS/IPS), and VPNs")
questions.explanation: Two networks with almost the same name suggests a fake "evil twin" hotspot. A network page has no reason to ask for a different site's password. That is credential harvesting. A VPN wouldn't help here: it encrypts your traffic, but it can't protect a password you type into a fake page yourself. Turning off the firewall removes protection.
questions.feedback: Fake hotspot. No Wi-Fi network needs your social media password. Ask staff, or use mobile data.
questions.learningObjective: Spot fake hotspots and understand the limits of VPNs.
choices: Don't enter it. Ask the staff for the real network name, and use mobile data for anything sensitive
Enter it, since cafés often ask you to log in
Try both networks until one works without a login
Turn off your firewall so the network connects faster
questions.subject: Scenario-Based
questions.body: At a café you see two networks: Kape_FreeWiFi and Kape_Free_WiFi. After you connect to one, a page says: "Log in with your SocialBook email and password to get internet access."

questions.curriculumRef: Cyber Forensics (BIT2226) — Mobile Device Forensics
questions.explanation: Text sender names (sender IDs) can be faked, and a faked one lands in the same thread as the real sender's messages. Where the message appears doesn't prove where it came from. The evidence is in the content: examplebank-ph.example isn't the trusted domain, and it threatens a same-day suspension. Many banks have also announced that they no longer send clickable links by text.
questions.feedback: Scam. Sender names can be faked, so the thread proves nothing. Check the link: it's not examplebank.example.
questions.learningObjective: Learn that what a phone displays is not proof of who sent a message.
questions.senderDetail: In the same thread as your real ExampleBank messages
questions.body: ExampleBank: Your account will be suspended TODAY. Update your details at

rooms.intro: Welcome to the Digital Forensics Lab.
lessons: Follow verification procedures under pressure from authority and urgency.
Recognize macro-enabled attachments and the "enable content" trick.
Understand that convincing personal details can come from public sources and don't prove the sender is real.
Read app permission requests and know that granting them can bypass passwords.
Verify high-risk requests through a separate channel, even when they come from trusted accounts.
Rank risks by likelihood and impact instead of by what seems most visible.

questions.curriculumRef: Social and Professional Issues (BIT2105). Supporting: Computer Security (BIT1225), Authentication and Access Control — Week 9: Ethics for IT Workers
questions.explanation: This is pretexting: a made-up story that uses authority and time pressure to get you to skip procedure. A reset sent to a personal address could hand the account to an attacker. An IT worker's duty is to follow verification even when it's uncomfortable. A real dean would understand.
questions.feedback: Verify first. Authority plus urgency is the oldest trick there is. Call back on the official number.
questions.learningObjective: Follow verification procedures under pressure from authority and urgency.
choices: Do it, because the dean outranks you
Reset it but send the password by SMS instead
Give the caller your own login for now
Follow the identity-verification procedure: call back on the dean's directory number, and send resets only to the official account
questions.subject: Scenario-Based
questions.body: You're a student assistant at the IT help desk. A caller says: "This is Dean Reyes. I'm locked out and presenting in five minutes. Reset my password and send it to my personal email, deanreyes.personal@freemail.example. Hurry!"

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Malware and Threats
questions.explanation: .docm files can contain macros, which are small programs. Office disables them by default for safety. Attackers make the document look empty or blurred so you click "Enable Content", which runs their code and can install malware. A grades file doesn't need macros to display.
questions.feedback: Macro trap. Enable Content = run their code. Grades don't need macros.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize macro-enabled attachments and the "enable content" trick.
choices: A normal Word update
A macro malware trap: enabling content runs hidden code
A corrupted file that needs repair
The document is just read-only
questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.body: An email titled "Revised grading sheet" has Grades_Final.docm attached. When opened, a yellow bar says: "Content is disabled. Click ENABLE CONTENT to view the grades." What's going on?

questions.curriculumRef: Advanced Cybersecurity Strategies (BIT4233) — Advanced Pen Testing (reconnaissance) and APT Defense (TTPs)
questions.explanation: The email uses real names, dates and events, which takes research. That is reconnaissance, the first stage of both attacks and penetration tests. A targeted message aimed at one person is spear phishing. It isn't clone phishing because no earlier real email was copied. The giveaways are the free-mail address, the "new account" and the same-day deadline.
questions.feedback: Spear phishing. They read your public page first. Real details don't mean a real sender.
questions.learningObjective: Understand that convincing personal details can come from public sources and don't prove the sender is real.
choices: Random spam sent to thousands of people
Clone phishing (a copy of an earlier real email)
Spear phishing built from public information gathered beforehand
Ransomware
questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.body: You're your student org's treasurer. Email from: "Prof. L. Santos" <lsantos.adviser@freemail.example> "Hi! As we discussed at Tuesday's meeting, please send the venue deposit for the Sept 14 Acquaintance Party to our new account before 3 PM today. Thanks!" Case file: The meeting, the date and the event were all posted on the org's public page. The adviser's school address is lsantos@uphsl-binan.example.

questions.curriculumRef: Advanced Cybersecurity Strategies (BIT4233) — Cloud Security ("identity management" in SaaS)
questions.explanation: This attack doesn't steal your password. It gets you to give a malicious app permanent access. A document viewer has no reason to send or delete your mail. Changing your password afterwards often doesn't remove an app's access, which stays until you remove the app from your account. The sign-in page being real is part of the trick.
questions.feedback: Cancel. The login was real, but the permissions were the trap. A viewer doesn't need to send your mail.
questions.learningObjective: Read app permission requests and know that granting them can bypass passwords.
choices: Cancel. It's a permission-granting (consent) phishing attempt. Report it and review your connected apps
Accept, because the sign-in page was real
Accept, then change your password afterwards to be safe
Accept just this once
questions.subject: Scenario-Based
questions.body: You open a "shared document" link. It takes you to the real NovaCloud sign-in page (novacloud.example). After you sign in, a screen appears: "DocuView Plus (unverified publisher) wants to: • Read, send and delete your mail • Access your files at any time • Keep access when you're not using it"

questions.curriculumRef: Advanced Cybersecurity Strategies (BIT4233) — Secure Network Design ("zero-trust models")
questions.explanation: When the director's account itself has been taken over, every technical check passes because the email really comes from that account. This is business email compromise. Replying goes straight to the attacker. Zero trust means never trust, always verify each request, especially a change of bank details, even when it comes from inside. "Don't call" is a warning sign in itself.
questions.feedback: Verify by phone, on a number you already have. A real account can still be controlled by an attacker.
questions.learningObjective: Verify high-risk requests through a separate channel, even when they come from trusted accounts.
choices: Pay it, since the email passed authentication and came from the real address
Reply to the email asking the director to confirm
Pay half now and half after confirming
Verify through a separate channel you already trust (the director's directory number and the supplier's number on file) before changing any bank details
questions.subject: What Should You Do?
questions.body: An email comes from the finance director's real address in an existing thread, and it passes all email authentication checks: "Our supplier changed banks. Please pay today's invoice (₱480,000) to the new account below. I'm in meetings all day, so don't call, just reply here."

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Weeks 13–14: Vulnerabilities and Risk Management ("conduct a basic risk assessment")
questions.explanation: Risk = likelihood × impact. The admin account is very likely to be exploited, because its password is already public and there's no second factor. The impact is severe: an admin email account controls everyone's mail. The other findings are real but lower on one or both factors. Staff training matters, but it doesn't close an open door right now.
questions.feedback: Fix the admin account first: public password + no MFA + admin access means high likelihood and high impact.
questions.learningObjective: Rank risks by likelihood and impact instead of by what seems most visible.
choices: Lab PCs are one month behind on non-security feature updates
The email administrator account has no MFA, and its password appears in a public breach list
The spam filter sometimes flags newsletters by mistake
Some staff haven't attended this year's awareness seminar yet
questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.body: After a phishing wave on campus, IT lists four findings. Which should be fixed first?

rooms.intro: The campus network has been compromised.
caseNotes: A "Scholarship Grant 2027" form is shared in a student group. It uses the school logo.
The canteen's "Scan to pay with PayLite" poster looks normal, but up close the QR code is a sticker placed on top of the printed one.
lessons: Keep evidence complete, unchanged and documented.
Use technical header evidence rather than what the email shows on the surface.
Separate normal data requests from identity-theft collection using DPA principles.
Know the first response steps: contain, preserve evidence, report.
Treat QR codes like links: check where they lead, and look for physical tampering.
Respond to discovered wrongdoing within your authority and without causing more harm.

questions.curriculumRef: Cyber Forensics (BIT2226) — Legal Aspects of Cyber Forensics ("maintaining evidence integrity"). Supporting: Digital Evidence and Evidence Collection
questions.explanation: Evidence has to be complete and unchanged to be trusted. Cropping removes context, and blurring removes the scammer's identifiers that investigators need. Keeping the original device and noting how you collected each item is a basic chain of custody. Uninstalling may delete the chat history. Group chats spread personal data.
questions.feedback: Keep the originals untouched, share copies, and write down when you saved each one.
questions.learningObjective: Keep evidence complete, unchanged and documented.
choices: Crop the screenshots to just the scam message and blur the scammer's name for privacy
Forward everything to a big group chat so more people can confirm it

Keep the full conversation untouched on the original phone. Take full screenshots showing the sender's profile or number with dates and times, save receipts with reference numbers, share only copies, and note when and how each item was collected
Uninstall the app to stop the scammer and write down what you remember
questions.subject: Scenario-Based
questions.body: A friend was scammed through a chat app and wants to file a report. Which way of handling the evidence is best?

questions.curriculumRef: Cyber Forensics (BIT2226) — Network Forensics and Cybercrime Investigation ("identify signs of cybercrimes")
questions.explanation: The "From" line can say anything, so the display name proves nothing. SPF/DMARC fail means the registrar's domain did not authorize the server that sent this email. The Reply-To quietly sends your answer to the attacker. The subject and time are only weak signs.
questions.feedback: SPF and DMARC failed, and replies go to free-mail. The 'From' name is just text anyone can type.
questions.learningObjective: Use technical header evidence rather than what the email shows on the surface.
choices: SPF and DMARC fail for the registrar's domain, and replies are redirected to a free-mail address
The subject mentions tuition
The display name says "Registrar's Office"
It was sent at 2:14 AM
questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.body: Email header excerpt: From: "Registrar's Office" <registrar@uphsl-binan.example> Reply-To: registrar.office.ph@freemail.example Return-Path: <bounce@mailer-xyz.example> Authentication-Results: spf=fail; dkim=none; dmarc=fail Subject: FINAL reminder: unpaid tuition, account on hold What is the strongest evidence that this is spoofed?

questions.curriculumRef: Social and Professional Issues (BIT2105) — Week 15: Data Privacy Act (RA 10173)
questions.explanation: Real scholarship offices sometimes do ask for ID, which is what makes this hard. The deciding signs are: (1) no one ever needs your MPIN to send you money; (2) an ID plus a selfie holding it is exactly what's needed to open accounts in your name; (3) there is no privacy notice and no official contact. That breaks the DPA principles of transparency and proportionality. Check through the scholarship office's official channel.
questions.feedback: Scam. No one needs your MPIN to pay you. With ID + selfie + MPIN, they can become you.
questions.learningObjective: Separate normal data requests from identity-theft collection using DPA principles.
questions.subject: Scholarship Grant 2027
questions.body:
Please provide: full name, student number, birthdate, mother's maiden name, front and back of your ID, a selfie holding your ID, and your PayLite MPIN "for fast release of funds".

There is no privacy notice. The only contact is a mobile number.
questions.scenarioContext: A "Scholarship Grant 2027" form is shared in a student group. It uses the school logo.

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Incident Response and Forensics
questions.explanation: First, contain it: cutting the network connection stops it spreading to shared drives and other PCs. Leaving the PC on keeps evidence in memory for investigators. Follow your organization's response plan if it says otherwise. Paying doesn't guarantee you'll get your files back. Restarting or cleaning can destroy evidence. Copying to a USB can spread the infection or copy already-locked files.
questions.feedback: Disconnect, don't shut down, report. Containment first; investigators need the evidence.
questions.learningObjective: Know the first response steps: contain, preserve evidence, report.
choices: Pay quickly before the price goes up
Disconnect the PC from the network (unplug the cable or turn off Wi-Fi), leave it on, stop using it, and report to IT or the incident team immediately
Restart, run a cleanup tool and delete the ransom note
Copy your files to your USB drive to save them
questions.subject: What Should You Do?
questions.body: After you open an email attachment on a lab PC, your files start changing to .locked and a note demands cryptocurrency. What do you do first?

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 17: Real-World Applications and Case Studies
questions.explanation: This is QR code phishing. A sticker over the original is the physical clue. A real merchant QR opens inside the e-wallet app and shows the merchant's name for you to confirm. It never asks for your MPIN on a web page. Also tell the canteen staff, so the next person doesn't get caught.
questions.feedback: Scam. Sticker over sticker, a browser page and an MPIN request. Real payments happen inside the app.
questions.learningObjective: Treat QR codes like links: check where they lead, and look for physical tampering.
questions.sender: Page opened by the canteen QR code
questions.subject: Scan to pay with PayLite
questions.body: Enter your mobile number and MPIN to pay.
questions.scenarioContext: The canteen's "Scan to pay with PayLite" poster looks normal, but up close the QR code is a sticker placed on top of the printed one.

questions.curriculumRef: Social and Professional Issues (BIT2105) — Week 16: Professional Organization and ACM Code of Ethics
questions.explanation: The ACM Code of Ethics asks computing professionals to avoid harm (1.2), respect privacy (1.6) and access computing resources only when authorized (2.8). Downloading the list means handling other people's stolen data without authorization. Posting the link sends more victims to it. Testing it hands over your own password. Reporting lets the people with authority act.
questions.feedback: Report it, don't touch it. Good intentions don't make unauthorized access okay.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to discovered wrongdoing within your authority and without causing more harm.
choices: Download the list and message each victim yourself
Post the link on the freedom wall to warn everyone
Test it with your own real password to confirm it works
Report it right away to the school's IT or security office with screenshots and the URL written in a non-clickable form (e.g., hxxp://), without logging in or using the captured data
questions.subject: Scenario-Based
questions.body: You find a fake school login page. Its admin page is publicly open and shows a list of student passwords it has captured. What is the ethical action?
